questions.question: What are CSS custom properties, and how does var() use them?
questions.title: CSS custom properties and var()
questions.direct_answer: CSS custom properties are author-defined properties whose names start with --. var() substitutes a custom property's computed value into another CSS declaration, with an optional fallback when the referenced value is missing or invalid.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands custom properties as live values in the cascade, not text macros.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling them compile-time variables or assuming a var() fallback repairs every invalid final value.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain computed-value substitution, inheritance, and one boundary of var().

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Custom property names begin with two hyphens, such as --brand-color.
var(--name) substitutes the selected custom-property value at computed-value time.
var(--name, fallback) uses the fallback when the reference is missing or invalid.
Custom properties participate in the cascade and normally inherit.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A CSS custom property is an author-defined property such as `--brand-color`. It stores a CSS token value on an element, and another declaration reads that value with `var(--brand-color)`. Because it is a real property, the cascade, selector matching, and inheritance decide which value an element receives.

Resolution happens when the browser computes the consuming declaration. If `color: var(--brand-color)` resolves to a usable color, that value becomes the text color. If the custom property is missing or has a guaranteed-invalid value, `var(--brand-color, navy)` substitutes `navy` instead.

For example, a card can inherit `--surface` from `:root`, while a warning container overrides the same property for all cards inside it. The component rule remains `background: var(--surface)`; only the scoped value changes.

A fallback is part of `var()`, not a general validator for the final property. A defined value such as `--brand-color: 20px` can still make `color` invalid because a length is not a color. Registering a property with `@property` can add a syntax, inheritance rule, and initial value when that control is needed.

I use custom properties for values that need to vary through the DOM or at runtime, such as theme colors, spacing choices, and component settings. They keep the relationship visible while normal CSS still decides the winning value.

sections.title: A value travels through the cascade
sections.content: The browser first finds the winning declaration for --brand-color on an element. If none is declared there, an unregistered custom property normally inherits its parent's computed value. Only then does var() substitute that value into color, background, or another consuming property.

sections.title: Why substitution can fail late
sections.content: Custom-property values accept a broad token stream, so `--accent: 12px` is valid as a custom-property declaration. The problem appears only when those tokens enter `color: var(--accent)`, where 12px does not satisfy the color grammar. With no usable result, the consuming declaration becomes invalid at computed-value time. A fallback handles an unavailable variable reference; `@property --accent { syntax: '<color>'; inherits: true; initial-value: navy; }` additionally constrains the custom property's type.

sections.title: From declaration to used style
sections.content: matching declarations → cascade chooses --accent → inheritance fills any gap → var() substitutes tokens → color grammar accepts or rejects them

sections.title: Scope one token without changing the component rule

questions.question: How do scope, the cascade, and inheritance affect CSS custom properties?
questions.title: Scoping and inheriting CSS custom properties
questions.direct_answer: A custom property can be declared on any element. The cascade chooses its winning declaration for that element, and an unregistered custom property inherits by default, so descendants can reuse or locally override a token without changing the component rule.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can trace a custom-property value through a real DOM tree.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating :root as mandatory or expecting a sibling's custom property to be visible.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish selector scope from lexical scope and mention @property inherits: false.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A declaration belongs to the elements matched by its selector.
Normal cascade rules choose among competing custom-property declarations.
Unregistered custom properties inherit to descendants by default.
Siblings do not inherit values from each other.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
CSS custom properties use DOM scope rather than the lexical scope of a programming language. A declaration on `:root` is available throughout the document because every element descends from the root, but a declaration on `.dialog` is available only on that element and its descendants.

If several matching rules assign `--space`, the cascade selects one for the current element using origin, importance, layer, specificity, and source order. When the element has no winning declaration, an unregistered custom property normally inherits the computed value from its parent.

For example, `:root` can provide a blue `--accent`, a `.danger-zone` can override it with red, and a button can keep using `background: var(--accent)`. Buttons outside the danger zone remain blue; buttons inside inherit red. A sibling of `.danger-zone` is unaffected because inheritance follows parent-to-child relationships.

The value is resolved where the custom property is used. A child can therefore combine an inherited token with its own local values. If a design token must not inherit, it can be registered with `@property` and `inherits: false`, along with a syntax and initial value.

This model makes component APIs possible: define sensible defaults high in the tree and override only at meaningful boundaries. I keep global tokens small and use component-level names for local behaviour so an override does not accidentally affect unrelated descendants.

sections.title: Scope follows the element tree
sections.content: Selectors decide where a value is declared; the cascade decides which declaration wins; inheritance carries that computed value downward. There is no sideways lookup between siblings and no upward lookup from a child to its parent.

sections.title: Fallbacks do not search arbitrary ancestors
sections.content: Inheritance already determines the custom property's value before var() is evaluated. `var(--accent, blue)` does not walk every ancestor or choose the fallback merely because the nearest ancestor omitted a declaration. It reads the computed --accent value on the current element, which may itself be inherited. Local overrides form deliberate boundaries, which is why theme containers work without rewriting component selectors.

sections.title: Inheritance path for one token
sections.content:
:root --accent: blue
├─ .page → inherits blue
│  ├─ .card → inherits blue
│  └─ .danger --accent: red
│     └─ .button → inherits red
└─ .footer → inherits blue

sections.title: Override a token at a meaningful boundary

questions.question: How would you implement light and dark themes with CSS custom properties?
questions.title: Theme switching with CSS custom properties
questions.direct_answer: Define semantic theme tokens once, consume them in components, and override the token values under a theme selector or prefers-color-scheme query. Changing one class or data attribute then updates every component that reads those inherited tokens.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can separate semantic design tokens from component styles.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating complete component rules for each theme or using color names as token names.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Cover system preference, an explicit user override, persistence, and readable contrast.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Name tokens by purpose, such as --surface and --text, not by a fixed color.
Components consume tokens and do not need theme-specific selectors.
A data attribute can represent an explicit user choice.
prefers-color-scheme can supply the initial system-aware theme.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I build themes around semantic custom properties such as `--surface`, `--text`, and `--accent`. Components use those names, so a card describes its role with `background: var(--surface)` instead of knowing whether the current theme uses white or charcoal.

The default values can live on `:root`. A media query for `prefers-color-scheme: dark` can provide a system-aware dark set, while an explicit selector such as `html[data-theme='dark']` represents a choice made in the application. JavaScript only needs to change that attribute; CSS performs the rest through inheritance.

For example, a user who selects dark mode gets the attribute saved in local storage. On the next visit, a small startup script restores it before the page paints, which avoids a flash of the wrong theme. Without a saved choice, the system preference remains the default.

Theme tokens still need design review. Swapping background colors does not automatically guarantee text contrast, visible focus indicators, readable disabled states, or suitable images. I test each supported theme rather than assuming token symmetry makes it accessible.

The useful boundary is that CSS owns visual values while application state owns the user's selection. This keeps theme logic small, lets components stay reusable, and makes a future high-contrast theme another token set instead of another copy of the UI.

sections.title: Components depend on meaning, not a palette
sections.content: A semantic token is a contract. `--surface` means the background that content sits on; its actual color may vary by theme. Theme selectors change the contract's values, while component selectors continue to express the same visual roles.

sections.title: Resolve automatic and explicit choices separately
sections.content: System preference is a useful default, but a product may also offer a manual choice. Give the explicit attribute rule a clear place after the automatic media rule so it wins predictably. Persist only the user's override; if no override exists, allow later operating-system changes to flow through. Set `color-scheme: light dark` when the page supports both so browser-provided controls can use an appropriate scheme too.

sections.title: Theme decision and token flow
sections.content:
saved user choice? ─ yes → data-theme values
        │
        no
        ↓
system preference → root token values → inherited by cards, forms, and navigation

sections.title: One component, two token sets

questions.question: What is the difference between CSS custom properties and Sass variables?
questions.title: CSS custom properties versus Sass variables
questions.direct_answer: Sass variables are replaced while Sass compiles, so they do not exist in the browser. CSS custom properties remain in the generated CSS, participate in cascade and inheritance, and can change at runtime through selectors, media queries, or JavaScript.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands compile-time substitution versus browser-resolved values.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling the two interchangeable because both reuse named values.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Choose each by whether the value needs runtime cascade behaviour or build-time calculation.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: CSS custom properties remain available to the browser.
Custom properties cascade, inherit, and can change at runtime.
Sass variables support build-time language features and can generate CSS.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Sass variables and CSS custom properties both give a value a name, but they run at different stages. Sass replaces `$gap` while building the stylesheet. The browser receives the resulting literal value and has no `$gap` variable to inspect or change.

A CSS custom property such as `--gap` remains in the stylesheet. The browser computes it for each element using selectors, the cascade, and inheritance, then substitutes it through `var(--gap)`. That makes it suitable for themes, container-specific component settings, and values changed by media queries or JavaScript.

For example, Sass can use a loop and a build-time variable to generate twelve spacing utility classes. CSS custom properties can then let one component change its current spacing at runtime without generating another class for every possible value.

Sass has richer build-time programming tools, but it cannot react to a DOM class unless the compiled CSS already contains a matching rule. CSS custom properties are runtime-friendly, but an unregistered property accepts broad token values and may fail only when used in a typed property.

I often use both: Sass for authoring structure or generating repetitive rules, and CSS custom properties for values that belong to the rendered page's state. The deciding question is not which syntax is newer; it is when and where the value must be resolved.

sections.title: Two variables, two execution times
sections.content: Sass works before deployment and emits ordinary CSS. Custom properties work inside the browser after selector matching and can differ for two elements on the same page. That timing difference determines almost every practical trade-off.

sections.title: The compiled output reveals the difference
sections.content: If `$space: 1rem` is used in ten Sass declarations, the compiled file normally contains ten copies of `1rem`. Changing the source requires another build. If `--space: 1rem` is referenced ten times, those references remain and can inherit a different computed value under a compact container. Build-time tools are still valuable for maps, loops, and file organization; runtime tokens are valuable when user state or DOM context must influence the result.

sections.title: Where each value exists
sections.content:
| Capability | Sass variable | CSS custom property |
|---|---|---|
| Resolved | During build | In the browser |
| Participates in cascade | No | Yes |
| Changes at runtime | Only through pre-generated rules | Yes |
| Generates repeated rules | Yes | No by itself |

sections.title: Keep runtime tokens in the compiled CSS
